lead: A definite integral needs a finite interval and a bounded integrand. If either fails, the integral is improper. Replace the bad end by a variable and take a limit: R→∞ for an infinite interval, or c→a⁺ for a function that blows up at a. The limit is the integral. This idea is used in probability densities with infinite support, in the gamma function, and in Laplace transforms. This chapter decides convergence without always finding a value, using p-integrals and comparison.
prereq: You need definite integrals and the fundamental theorem, integration techniques, and limits.

blocks.text: An improper integral is a limit of proper integrals. First kind: the interval is infinite. For a function f continuous on [a, ∞), define ∫ₐ^∞ f(x) dx = lim R→∞ ∫ₐ^R f(x) dx. R is a real number with R > a. If the limit is a finite real number, the integral converges; otherwise it diverges. A similar definition holds for (−∞, b]. Some syllabi call these improper integrals of the first kind.

Second kind: the integrand is unbounded. If f blows up at b and is continuous on [a, b), define ∫ₐ^b f(x) dx = lim c→b⁻ ∫ₐ^c f(x) dx. Here c approaches b from below. If f blows up at a, use c→a⁺. If f blows up at an interior point, split the interval at that point. Both pieces must converge. Take the limit after integration, never by substituting ∞ or the blow-up point as a number.

For a real constant p, the two p-integrals are the reference tests. ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges exactly when p > 1. For p ≠ 1, ∫ x^(−p) dx = x^(1−p)/(1−p). At R, x^(1−p)/(1−p) tends to 0 when 1−p < 0, that is when p > 1, giving the value 0 − 1/(1−p) = 1/(p−1). When p < 1, 1−p > 0 and the expression grows without bound. For p=1, ∫₁^R x⁻¹ dx = ln R, which tends to ∞. Hence p=1 diverges.

∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx converges exactly when p < 1. For p ≠ 1, the proper integral from c to 1 equals 1/(1−p) − c^(1−p)/(1−p). For p < 1, c^(1−p) → 0 as c→0⁺, so the limit is 1/(1−p). For p > 1, 1−p < 0 and c^(1−p) grows without bound. For p = 1, the value ln(1/c) grows. Hence p = 1 diverges. The rules look opposite because the intervals are opposite: near ∞, a larger p makes x^(−p) decay faster; near 0, a smaller p makes x^(−p) blow up more slowly.

Comparison test. Let f and g be positive on the same improper interval, with 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x). If ∫g converges, then ∫f converges. If ∫f diverges, then ∫g diverges. The reason is monotonicity: the proper integral of a positive f increases as R grows or as c moves toward the blow-up point. If it stays below a finite bound, it has a finite limit. Compare with a p-integral whose exponent you can read.

Example: ∫₁^∞ 1/(x²+1) dx converges because 1/(x²+1) ≤ 1/x² and ∫₁^∞ x^(−2) dx converges (p=2). Absolute convergence: if ∫|f(x)| dx converges, then ∫f(x) dx converges. Call the original integral absolutely convergent. The converse fails: an integral can converge without its absolute version converging. Test absolute convergence first when signs oscillate; if it fails, the original may still converge, so check separately. The comparison and absolute-convergence statements hold for both kinds.

examples.question: Show that ∫₁^∞ x^(−2) dx converges and find its value.
steps: The upper limit is infinite, so write the definition: I = lim R→∞ ∫₁^R x^(−2) dx, with R > 1.
An antiderivative is −x^(−1), because d/dx(−x^(−1)) = x^(−2).
The limit is finite, so the improper integral converges. Its value is 1 square unit.
examples.answer: The integral converges to 1 square unit.

traps: Treating ∞ as a number and writing F(∞) − F(1) directly. Write a limit and take it after integration.
Checking only one bad endpoint. If the integrand blows up inside the interval, split there and test both pieces.
Mixing the p-rules: ∫₁^∞ x^(−p) dx converges for p > 1, but ∫₀¹ x^(−p) dx converges for p < 1.
Using comparison in the wrong direction. A smaller divergent integrand proves nothing; a larger convergent integrand proves nothing.
Assuming absolute convergence is necessary for convergence. For oscillating integrands, the original may converge while ∫|f| diverges.

quiz.q: State the limit definition of ∫ₐ^∞ f(x) dx.
quiz.a: ∫ₐ^∞ f(x) dx = lim R→∞ ∫ₐ^R f(x) dx, when the limit is a finite real number.

quiz.q: Why does ∫₁^∞ x^(−1) dx diverge by the p-test?
quiz.a: Here p=1, the boundary case. ∫₁^R x⁻¹ dx = ln R, and ln R tends to ∞ as R→∞.

quiz.q: Use the p-test to decide convergence and value for ∫₀¹ x^(−1/2) dx.
quiz.a: p=1/2<1, so it converges. ∫₀¹ x^(−1/2) dx = [2√x]₀¹ = 2.

quiz.q: For positive f and g with f(x) ≤ g(x), if ∫g diverges, what can you conclude about ∫f? Explain.
quiz.a: Nothing. A larger integral diverging does not force the smaller one to diverge; the smaller integral may converge or diverge.
For x≥1, x+1≤2x and x³+2≥x³, so the integrand ≤ 2x/x³ = 2/x². Since ∫₁^∞ 2x^(−2) dx converges (p=2), the given integral converges by comparison.

quiz.q: An integrand blows up at x=1 inside [0,2]. How do you define the improper integral?
quiz.a: Split: ∫₀¹ f dx + ∫₁² f dx. Write lim c→1⁻ ∫₀^c f dx and lim d→1⁺ ∫_d² f dx. Both limits must be finite; if either diverges, the whole integral diverges.

quiz.q: Does absolute convergence imply convergence for improper integrals? Does the converse hold?
quiz.a: Yes, ∫|f| convergent implies ∫f convergent. The converse fails; a conditionally convergent improper integral can converge while its absolute version diverges.

beyond: Not for the exam. Improper integrals underpin probability densities on infinite ranges, the gamma function, and Laplace transforms. In numerical work they are handled by variable changes or by truncating a tail and estimating the error. Search next for comparison test for improper integrals, absolute convergence, and gamma function convergence.
